title: Six-week plan to learn ladder logic well enough for a controls tech interview
summary: Six weeks of small ladder-logic builds, fault injections and explanations.

blocks.heading: Leave with one program you can defend
blocks.body: Plan assumption: four 45-minute sessions each week, using one simulator or training environment. The outcome is a small simulated conveyor sequence, a test record and a clear explanation of failure behavior. Six weeks does not qualify someone to alter a live machine or its safety system.

blocks.heading: Build something observable every week
rows: 1 · Bits and scan
Start/stop command with a simulated permissive
Explain why each contact evaluates true or false; restart behavior is deliberate
2 · Time
Delay a simulated conveyor start, cancel on lost permissive
Trace elapsed time and done state across enable, disable and re-enable
3 · Edges and counts
Count one simulated part per sensor event
A held input does not count every scan; explain missed short pulses
4 · Sequence
Idle → starting → running → fault
One active state; defined transitions; no accidental restart after a fault
5 · Diagnostics
Inject a stuck sensor, missing permissive and timeout
State expected vs observed behavior and identify a useful next check
6 · Interview evidence
Demonstrate, test and explain the complete project
Another person can reproduce the scenario from your instructions

blocks.heading: A 45-minute session
items: 5 min: predict the program’s next state before running it.
20 min: build one small change and observe its variables.
10 min: deliberately break one assumption in simulation.
10 min: write the result, the explanation and the next question.

blocks.heading: Contacts examine bits; field devices create signals
blocks.body: A normally closed field switch and an instruction that tests a bit for zero are different ideas. First establish the electrical signal at the input, then the stored bit, then the instruction’s truth result. This is why a drawing symbol alone does not tell you what the program will do.

blocks.heading: Make execution order visible
blocks.body: For a simple cyclic teaching model, copy inputs, execute rungs in order and update outputs. Real controllers may use periodic/event tasks and asynchronous I/O; check the platform’s documentation. Ask what a later rung sees after an earlier rung writes a tag, and avoid multiple writers until you can explain their effect.

blocks.heading: Keep this fault matrix with the project
rows: Power-up with Start held
No unexpected motion command under your specified startup policy
Initial values and first two scans
Permissive drops while running
Run command removed; fault response follows the specification
State transition and output tag
Sensor stays high
Single event count, not one count per scan
Counter and edge-storage values
Sequence exceeds deadline
Timeout state with a specific diagnostic
Timer and transition condition
Fault reset while Start held
Reset alone does not start the process
Separate reset and new-start events
blocks.caption: This is a simulated functional control exercise. Safety-rated stopping and restart prevention require a separate engineered safety design.

items.label: Keep the test record
items.detail: Reduce the number of features before removing evidence.

items.label: Repeat a weak week
items.detail: Do not add counters if the scan model is still a guess.

items.label: Use one platform through the project
items.detail: Learn its exact timer, edge and initialization behavior before translating to another.

blocks.heading: A useful two-minute demonstration
blocks.body: State the requirement, run the normal sequence, inject one fault, and explain what proves the program responded correctly. Finish with one limitation you have not solved. Bring the program, a short I/O list and the test matrix; “it worked once” is not the evidence.

items.label: Rockwell Automation: bit instructions
items.detail: One vendor’s instruction semantics. Use your chosen simulator/controller manual for exact behavior.
